extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and news organisations (particularly in Australia) subject to Australian Press Council standards
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and adjudication guidance for news organisations on presenting factual material fairly, avoiding prejudicial emphasis on personal characteristics, and balancing potential harm against public interest in news reporting. Focused on reporting of crime and parole matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure factual material is presented with reasonable fairness and balance (General Principle 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that factual material is presented with reasonable fairness and balance, and that writers’ expressions of opinion are not based on significantly inaccurate factual material or omission of key facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications must take reasonable steps to verify facts and present them in a balanced way. The Council found the publication failed this standard where it prominently referenced an accomplice's transgender status that was irrelevant to the crime and included assertions (e.g. that the accomplice was "harbouring a desire to become a woman" at the time) without information to support them. Editors should remove or avoid irrelevant personal details and ensure opinions are not founded on significantly inaccurate facts or omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice unless public interest justifies it (General Principle 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice, or a substantial risk to health or safety, unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing material that may offend or prejudice a group or individual, weigh the harm against the public interest. The Council accepted there was public interest in reporting a parole hearing for a serious crime but concluded that prominent references to irrelevant transgender status were not sufficiently justified by public interest and could contribute to prejudice. Publications must justify any potentially prejudicial detail by a clear and sufficient public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not place unwarranted emphasis on characteristics (race, gender, sexual orientation, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications should exercise great care not to place unwarranted emphasis on characteristics of individuals such as race, religion, nationality, country of origin, gender, sexual orientation, marital status, disability, illness or age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid highlighting personal characteristics unless they are relevant to the story. The Council criticised the articles for prominent references to the accomplice's transgender status when it was irrelevant to the crime, noting such emphasis can lead readers to infer an inappropriate causal link and contribute to prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and report relevance of personal/background details to the matter being reported
rubrics_metrics.description: Only include personal or background details (such as gender identity, medical history, or other sensitive traits) when they are factually relevant to the reported event or necessary for public understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case the accomplice transitioned after the crime; the Council noted the transgender references were irrelevant and there was no information to support claims the accomplice 'harboured a desire to become a woman' at the time. Journalists should verify timing and relevance of such details and avoid presenting them in ways that imply causation without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest balancing: require sufficient public interest to justify potentially harmful detail
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story contains material that could cause offence, distress or prejudice, publications must demonstrate that including that material is sufficiently justified by the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council recognises serious public interest in informing the public about parole hearings for serious crimes, but found that the specific, prominent transgender references in these articles were not sufficiently justified. Editors should document and be prepared to explain why sensitive or potentially prejudicial details are necessary for the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take reasonable steps to comply with standards at the time of publication; post-publication remedies do not absolve initial failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications are obliged to take reasonable steps to comply with the Council's Standards of Practice at the time of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the Council welcomed subsequent amendments to remove irrelevant references and newsroom education, it emphasised that corrective action after publication and training do not excuse failures to meet standards at publication. Newsrooms should have processes (editing, fact-checking, training) in place to prevent breaches before publication.
